facts.statement: Wimanius is a genus of ichthyosaur that includes only one species, Wimanius odontopalatus.
facts.quote: Wimanius is a genus of ichthyosaur from the Middle Triassic of Switzerland, containing a single species, Wimanius odontopalatus.

facts.statement: The genus was described by Michael Maisch and Andreas Matzke in 1998 from an incomplete skull found at Monte San Giorgio on the Swiss-Italian border.
facts.quote: It was described by Michael Maisch and Andreas Matzke in 1998 based on an incomplete skull from Monte San Giorgio, a mountain on the Swiss-Italian border.

facts.statement: Wimanius has teeth on its palate, but scientists disagree on whether these teeth sit on the palatine or pterygoid bone.
facts.quote: Wimanius possesses teeth on its palate, though whether they were located on the palatine or pterygoid is disputed.

facts.statement: Wimanius is characterized by a large eye socket and jugal bones with two arms of equal length.
facts.quote: Other features of Wimanius include a large orbit and jugals with two rami of similar lengths.

facts.statement: Studies have placed Wimanius as a mixosaurid relative or a merriamosaur, and a family named Wimaniidae was created for it.
facts.quote: Different phylogenetic placements of Wimanius have been recovered by different studies, including it being a mixosaurid relative or a merriamosaur, and a monotypic family, Wimaniidae has been named for it.

facts.statement: The validity of Wimanius is debated, with some researchers suggesting it should be merged with other genera.
facts.quote: However, its validity has also been questioned, and synonymy with various other genera has been proposed.

facts.statement: During the Anisian stage, the region where Wimanius lived was a lagoon inhabited by diverse marine life, including other ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: During the Anisian, this region was a lagoon populated by a wide variety of marine life, including a variety of other ichthyosaurs.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Wimanius was identified as a new genus by Maisch and Matzke while they were studying Mixosaurus fossils at the University of Tübingen.
facts.quote: The type and only specimen of Wimanius was first recognized as belonging to a new genus by Michael Maisch and Andreas Matzke while examining Mixosaurus specimens in the Museum für Geologie und Paläontologie der Universität Tübingen.

facts.statement: The genus name Wimanius honors the Swedish paleontologist Carl Wiman for his work on Triassic ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: The genus name Wimanius honors the Swedish paleontologist Carl Wiman, known for his numerous works concerning Triassic ichthyosaurs.

facts.statement: The species name odontopalatus refers to the unusual presence of teeth on the palate, which is rare for ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: The specific name odontopalatus refers to the presence of teeth on the palate, an unusual feature for an ichthyosaur.

facts.statement: The jugal bone of Wimanius consists of two arms of equal length that meet at a 110-degree angle.
facts.quote: The jugal is a thin bone, consisting of two rami of the same length that intersect in a curved, 110-degree angle.

facts.statement: Maisch and Matzke reconstructed Wimanius as having proportionally the largest eye sockets of any Triassic ichthyosaur, making the back of its skull quite tall.
facts.quote: Maisch and Matzke found Wimanius to have had very large orbits, proportionally the largest known among Triassic ichthyosaurs at the time, resulting in the back part of the skull being rather tall.

facts.statement: Based on the size of the eye socket, researchers estimated that Wimanius had a scleral ring containing 13 or 14 bony plates.
facts.quote: A circle of bony plates within the orbit known as the scleral ring would have supported the eye; while only two of these plates are known in the holotype, Maisch and Matzke estimated that a complete ring would have 13 or 14 in total based on their reconstructed orbit size.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of the Wimanius holotype measures about 25 cm, suggesting the animal was relatively small.
facts.quote: The lower jaw of Wimanius measures around 25 cm in the holotype, indicating that the animal was probably rather small.

facts.statement: All teeth in Wimanius were straight and cone-shaped, each set into its own socket.
facts.quote: The teeth of Wimanius are all straight and cone-shaped, with each tooth being set into a distinct socket.

facts.statement: The most complete tooth of Wimanius is about 1 mm tall, featuring a smooth conical crown and a coarse root.
facts.quote: The most complete of these teeth is only about 1 mm tall, with a smooth-sided conical crown and a coarse root.

facts.statement: In Wimanius, teeth were smaller at the front of the jaw and larger toward the back.
facts.quote: In both jaws, tooth size is smaller at the front and larger at the back.

facts.statement: The genus Wimanius was named in 1998 by Maisch and Matzke based on a fragmentary specimen.
facts.quote: In their 1998 paper naming Wimanius, Maisch and Matzke noted that the fragmentary nature of the only known specimen made it difficult to determine how to classify it with much confidence.

facts.statement: Motani classified Wimanius as Ichthyosauria incertae sedis in 1999.
facts.quote: In 1999, Motani classified Wimanius as Ichthyosauria incertae sedis.

facts.statement: Paul Martin Sander expressed doubt about the validity of Wimanius in 2000, suggesting further study was needed.
facts.quote: In 2000, Paul Martin Sander also expressed doubt over whether Wimanius was valid and stated that further study would be needed on the ichthyosaurs of the region to determine this.

facts.statement: Maisch and Matzke considered Wimanius a valid taxon in 2000, placing it as the sister taxon of Mixosauridae.
facts.quote: However, Maisch and Matzke considered Wimanius to be a valid, diagnosable taxon in 2000, including it in their phylogenetic analysis and finding it to be the sister taxon of Mixosauridae.

facts.statement: Motani considered Wimanius and Mikadocephalus to be potential junior synonyms of Pessosaurus in 2003.
facts.quote: In a 2003 book with Christopher McGowan, Motani considered that both Wimanius and Mikadocephalus might be junior synonyms of the taxonomically problematic Pessosaurus.

facts.statement: Maisch established the family Wimaniidae in 2010 to include Wimanius and mixosaurids.
facts.quote: In 2010, Maisch named a new monotypic family, Wimaniidae, using the name Mixosauria for the group consisting of it and mixosaurids.

facts.statement: Ben Moon's 2017 phylogenetic analysis placed Wimanius within the derived group Merriamosauria.
facts.quote: The phylogenetic analyses of Ben Moon in 2017 found a different placement for Wimanius, among the more derived group Merriamosauria.

facts.statement: Christian Klug and colleagues maintained Wimanius as a distinct and valid taxon in 2024.
facts.quote: In 2024, in a review detailing ichthyosaurs discovered in Switzerland, Christian Klug and colleagues maintain Wimanius as a distinct and valid ichthyosaur taxon pending re-evaluation.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Wimanius comes from the Besano Formation in Switzerland.
facts.quote: The only currently known specimen of Wimanius is recorded from the Besano Formation, also known as the Grenzbitumenzone in Switzerland.

facts.statement: Wimanius lived during the Late Triassic, specifically from the end of the Anisian to the beginning of the Ladinian stages.
facts.quote: This formation is located in the Alps and extends from southern Switzerland to northern Italy, containing numerous fossils dating from between the end of the Anisian and the beginning of the Ladinian.

facts.statement: Wimanius inhabited a marine lagoon in the western Tethys Ocean during the Late Triassic.
facts.quote: During the time when the animal lived, when the Besano Formation was being deposited, the region where Monte San Giorgio is would have been a marine lagoon, located in a basin on the western side of the Tethys Ocean.

facts.statement: The marine lagoon where Wimanius lived was estimated to be between 30 and 130 meters deep.
facts.quote: Researchers estimate that this same lagoon would have reached between 30 – 130 m deep.

facts.statement: The surface waters of Wimanius' habitat were well-oxygenated and rich in plankton and free-swimming organisms.
facts.quote: The near-surface waters would have been well oxygenated and were inhabited by a wide range of plankton and free-swimming organisms.

facts.statement: Poor water circulation in Wimanius' habitat led to anoxic conditions at the bottom of the lagoon.
facts.quote: However, water circulation within the lagoon was poor, resulting in typically anoxic water at the bottom, deprived of oxygen.

facts.statement: Fossils of conifers and land-dwelling reptiles indicate that Wimanius lived near land.
facts.quote: The presence of terrestrial fossils, such as conifers and land-dwelling reptiles indicates that the region would have been near land.

facts.statement: The bivalve Daonella was one of the most common invertebrates in Wimanius' habitat.
facts.quote: Among the most common of the invertebrates from the Besano Formation is the bivalve Daonella.

facts.statement: Cephalopods such as nautiloids, coleoids, and ammonites were present in Wimanius' environment.
facts.quote: Cephalopods present include nautiloids, coleoids, and the especially common ammonites.

facts.statement: Wimanius' habitat contained a diverse array of bony fish, including abundant small species and larger representatives like Saurichthys.
facts.quote: A very large number of bony fish have been recorded in this formation. Many bony fish have been recorded in this formation, with actinopterygians being quite diverse, including abundant small species as well as larger representatives like Saurichthys, though rarer sarcopterygian coelacanths were also present.

facts.statement: Cartilaginous fish in Wimanius' habitat were uncommon and mainly consisted of hybodonts.
facts.quote: The cartilaginous fish of the Besano Formation are uncommon as well and mainly consist of hybodonts.

facts.statement: Other ichthyosaurs found in the same formation as Wimanius include Mixosaurus, Phalarodon, Besanosaurus, and Cymbospondylus.
facts.quote: Aside from Wimanius, the other ichthyosaurs that have been discovered in the Besano Formation include the small Mixosaurus and Phalarodon as well as the imposing Besanosaurus and Cymbospondylus.

facts.statement: Sauropterygians such as shell-crushing placodonts, pachypleurosaurs, and nothosaurids lived alongside Wimanius.
facts.quote: Various sauropterygians are known from the Besano Formation, including the shell-crushing placodonts Paraplacodus and Cyamodus as well as pachypleurosaurs and nothosaurids.

facts.statement: Marine reptiles like thalattosaurs and Tanystropheus coexisted with Wimanius in the Besano Formation.
facts.quote: Besides ichthyosaurs and sauropterygians, marine reptiles in the Besano Formation are represented by the thalattosaurs Askeptosaurus, Clarazia, and Hescheleria in addition to the semiaquatic, long-necked Tanystropheus.

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Wimanius is Wimanius odontopalatus.
facts.quote: Type species: Wimanius odontopalatus

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Wimanius has been recorded.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 1
